newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian republic push bursts back to life.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian republic push bursts back to life.

text.p: The push for Australia to become a republic has burst back to life with renewed calls for a national vote on the issue this year, amid charges that monarchist Prime Minister John Howard is allowing the issue die.

"We feel that the time has come for the government now to match its populist rhetoric to political reality and to have a plebiscite," Malcolm Turnbull, chairman of the Australian Republican Movement, said on Tuesday.
Liberal leader Howard, who ousted republican Labor prime minister Paul Keating last March, made an election promise to hold a people's convention and plebiscite on the republican issue in 1997.
But media reports say the government is planning to water down the convention, allowing the national and state governments to elect all delegates, and possibly delay it until 1998.
"If John Howard wants to be taken seriously as being committed to democracy then the people's convention should be chosen by the people," Turnbull said at a news conference.

"I'm very concerned that it's become a delaying tactic. It (the government) promised a people's convention in 1997. We are now in 1997 and we don't have the faintest idea what they're intending," Turnbull said.
But Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer on Tuesday denied the government was moving too slowly towards a promised vote on removing Britain's Queen Elizabeth as head-of-state.
"This is a second-order issue as we seek to boost our export effort, as we seek to ensure job creation across the country," Fischer told reporters.
Fischer said he was confident the government would set up a people's convention and a plebiscite on the republic issue.
The convention aims to produce options to be voted on in a national plebiscite, but this vote would not be binding on the government.
To change the Australian constitution to allow a republic, a majority of Australians in a majority of the country's six states must support a referendum favouring a republic.
Howard's cabinet discussed its republic plans on Tuesday at its first meeting for the year and republicans are watching closely to see whether the government waters down any of its election promises.
"It is disturbing that nearly a year since it was elected, the Howard government is overdue in announcing its programme," New South Wales Opposition Leader Peter Collins said on Monday.

"The perception is growing, I trust wrongly, that the federal govenment is reneging on its promises, which could become politically damaging," said Collins, a republican member of Howard's Liberal party.
Opinion polls show about half of Australians want a republic but also that they think the country faces more pressing problems. Many are uncommitted.
Keating began his republican push shortly after he became prime minister in 1992 and the country became focussed on the issue for a few years.

Keating hoped to replace Queen Elizabeth with an Australian president either before the Sydney Olympic Games in 2000 or on January 1, 2001, the centenary of Australia's federation from six British colonies.

During the past 12 months the republican issue faded from the political arena. But the 1997 Australian of the Year, Peter Doherty, rekindled the debate on Australia Day, January 26, when he called for a republic.

"I don't see any reason for maintaining a situation in which the head of state of Australia is the Queen of England," said Doherty, a medical researcher who jointly won the Nobel prize for medicine in 1996.
